power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Work-life balance policies can redistribute time without transferring responsibility for anticipating and coordinating care.
This conceptual article asks when changes in time and task allocation permit caregivers to stop monitoring care needs.

Integrating research on cognitive household labor, work-family resources, psychological recovery, and social care, it develops a model linking responsibility, authority, and the opportunity to disengage.
The model proposes that continued answerability sustains monitoring and anticipatory vigilance even when another person performs the associated tasks.
A dependable successor, understood as a person or institution able to assume responsibility for a defined care need, is proposed as one relational condition supporting disengagement.
Gender, socioeconomic conditions, family composition, institutional recognition, and workplace arrangements shape access to this condition.
The contribution is to specify how responsibility is retained or transferred within broader accounts of demands and resources, rather than to treat those accounts as exclusively concerned with time.
Testable propositions distinguish changes in task performance from changes in monitoring, identify boundary conditions, and guide research across care arrangements.

Using European work-life balance provisions as an illustrative policy context, the article proposes indicators for evaluating whether leave, flexibility, and services redistribute cognitive responsibility and support recovery, alongside their effects on participation in employment.
One parent takes a child to a medical appointment; the other has noticed the symptoms, arranged the visit, prepared the information, and remains responsible for checking the outcome.
The first parent performs the appointment task, while the second continues to monitor it.
If a workplace policy gives the first parent time off, task time may change hands without an equivalent transfer of coordinating responsibility.
This example raises the central question of this article: under what conditions does redistributing time and tasks also transfer responsibility for anticipating, organizing, and monitoring care?

Research on cognitive household labor establishes why this distinction matters: the activities that keep care functioning are not adequately represented by counts of visible tasks or hours (Daminger, 2019; Dean et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Research on cognitive household labor establishes why this distinction matters: the activities that keep care functioning are not adequately represented by counts of visible tasks or hours <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Daminger, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Dean et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The problem extends beyond the household because work-life balance policy acts predominantly through time.

In the European Union, Directive (EU) 2019/1158 establishes minimum rights to paternity, parental, and carers' leave and provides for requests for flexible working arrangements (European Parliament & Council of the European Union, 2019).
text.formatted: In the European Union, Directive (EU) 2019/1158 establishes minimum rights to paternity, parental, and carers' leave and provides for requests for flexible working arrangements (European Parliament & Council of the European Union, 2019).

text.text: These instruments widen access to employment and create conditions for sharing care.
Whether the time they make available also transfers responsibility for care is a separate question, and it lies beyond the reach of common indicators, which record hours and leave uptake.
If responsibility can remain in place while time is redistributed, predominantly temporal instruments may be insufficient on their own to reduce the strain that responsibility produces.
Existing research gives reasons to expect such persistence.

Cognitive labor persists when physical household labor declines: women's employment and earnings are associated with less physical household work and with no comparable reduction in cognitive labor (Weeks et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Cognitive labor persists when physical household labor declines: women's employment and earnings are associated with less physical household work and with no comparable reduction in cognitive labor <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Weeks et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Responsibility for anticipating and monitoring care is often held apart from the power to decide (Daminger, 2019), and responsibility appears more consequential for well-being than the performance of particular tasks (Ciciolla & Luthar, 2019).
text.formatted: Responsibility for anticipating and monitoring care is often held apart from the power to decide <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Daminger, 2019)</ref>, and responsibility appears more consequential for well-being than the performance of particular tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ciciolla & Luthar, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Time spent in other activities does not reliably release caregivers from family concerns either, since thinking about family matters continues during the working day and carries costs that differ between mothers and fathers (Offer, 2014).
text.formatted: Time spent in other activities does not reliably release caregivers from family concerns either, since thinking about family matters continues during the working day and carries costs that differ between mothers and fathers <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Offer, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings describe a demand that is held through answerability, that moves independently of task time, and that follows the caregiver into paid work.
Established theories provide substantial resources for answering this question.

Job demandsresources theory (Bakker & Demerouti, 2017) and the work-home resources model (ten Brummelhuis & Bakker, 2012) encompass psychological demands, contextual resources, and conditions that shape their consequences.
text.formatted: Job demandsresources theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bakker & Demerouti, 2017)</ref> and the work-home resources model <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(ten Brummelhuis & Bakker, 2012)</ref> encompass psychological demands, contextual resources, and conditions that shape their consequences.

text.text: The stressor-detachment model explains why continuing engagement with demands can impede recovery (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2015).
text.formatted: The stressor-detachment model explains why continuing engagement with demands can impede recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Sonnentag & Fritz, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These approaches can accommodate mental load and do not imply that equal hours produce equal strain.
The more specific task pursued here is to explain how responsibility remains attached to one caregiver when tasks change hands, and which arrangements allow that person to relinquish monitoring.
This requires specifying the allocation and transfer of a demand, alongside its intensity and the resources available to meet it.
The article develops a three-level model of care-related mental load.
Structural antecedents include social position, institutional and workplace resources, and the distribution of responsibility, authority, and the opportunity to disengage.
Psychological mechanisms include persistent monitoring, anticipatory vigilance, and difficulty detaching.
Proposed consequences include distress, exhaustion, work-family interference, and insufficient recovery.

The focal contribution is a relational account of transfer: a dependable successor is a person or institution that credibly assumes responsibility for a defined care need, including follow-up and foreseeable contingencies.
This is proposed as one condition supporting disengagement, rather than as a new name for all forms of social support or the only possible route to recovery.
Workplaces and public services help determine whether such transfers are possible.
Schedule control, supervisor support, institutional contact routines, and reliable care provision can change who is reachable, who can make decisions, and who must respond when an arrangement fails.
The model therefore connects household coordination to organizations and policy.
Five propositions, with subpropositions, identify testable pathways, and an evaluation matrix translates them into questions about leave, flexibility, workplace practices, and support services.
The argument is conceptual, and its proposed mechanisms require empirical evaluation.
European work-life balance policy provides an illustrative institutional context.
The model concerns the design of care arrangements; it does not estimate the effects of the European directive or establish that its provisions have failed.
Applications elsewhere should examine the relevant local institutions and entitlements.
This article develops a conceptual model through a targeted integration of published scholarship.
Its starting point is a distinction established in research on household labor: performing a task and retaining responsibility for its completion are not necessarily the same activity.

The argument brings that distinction into conversation with resource, boundary, recovery, and social care theories to specify how monitoring can persist or be relinquished (Daly & Lewis, 2000; Daminger, 2019; Dean et al., 2022; ten Brummelhuis & Bakker, 2012; Sonnentag & Fritz, 2015).
text.formatted: The argument brings that distinction into conversation with resource, boundary, recovery, and social care theories to specify how monitoring can persist or be relinquished <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Daly & Lewis, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Daminger, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Dean et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">ten Brummelhuis & Bakker, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Sonnentag & Fritz, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The analysis proceeds by defining the care relations at issue, comparing them with neighboring constructs, and deriving propositions about changes in task performance, answerability, and monitoring.
The cited studies supply evidence about relevant associations and conceptual distinctions; they do not constitute a systematically searched or pooled body of evidence.
Where a proposed mechanism extends findings from another setting, that extension is identified as a hypothesis.
European leave and flexibility provisions are used to illustrate policy implications, not as data from an evaluation of implementation.
The resulting framework is judged by conceptual clarity, consistency with existing evidence, and the availability of empirical comparisons that could support or challenge its added value.
Daminger (2019) identified cognitive household labor in four activities: anticipating needs, identifying options, deciding between them, and monitoring outcomes.

Subsequent work has extended this description. Robertson et al. (2019) define mental labor as thinking activity performed for the sake of accomplishing family goals and, from focus groups with mothers of young children, identify six forms: planning and strategizing, monitoring and anticipating needs, metaparenting, knowing, managerial thinking, and self-regulation. Dean et al. (2022) describe the combination of cognitive and emotional labor as invisible, persistent, and able to extend across work and non-work settings, and Wayne et al. (2023) distinguish managerial, cognitive, and emotional dimensions of invisible family load and report both costs and benefits across them.

(2019)</ref> define mental labor as thinking activity performed for the sake of accomplishing family goals and, from focus groups with mothers of young children, identify six forms: planning and strategizing, monitoring and anticipating needs, metaparenting, knowing, managerial thinking, and self-regulation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Dean et al. (2022)</ref> describe the combination of cognitive and emotional labor as invisible, persistent, and able to extend across work and non-work settings, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Wayne et al. (2023)</ref> distinguish managerial, cognitive, and emotional dimensions of invisible family load and report both costs and benefits across them.

text.text: A systematic review of 31 studies concluded that women carry the larger share of this work, particularly when they are not employed or work part time, and that the imbalance is associated with emotional strain, dissatisfaction, and career disadvantages (Reich-Stiebert et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A systematic review of 31 studies concluded that women carry the larger share of this work, particularly when they are not employed or work part time, and that the imbalance is associated with emotional strain, dissatisfaction, and career disadvantages <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Reich-Stiebert et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence on the consequences of this work points to responsibility as the component that matters most for well-being.

In a sample of 393 partnered mothers, Ciciolla and Luthar (2019) found that nearly nine in 10 reported being solely responsible for organizing family schedules, and that responsibility for children's well-being was the strongest predictor of feelings of emptiness and of lower satisfaction with life and with the partner relationship.
text.formatted: In a sample of 393 partnered mothers, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Ciciolla and Luthar (2019)</ref> found that nearly nine in 10 reported being solely responsible for organizing family schedules, and that responsibility for children's well-being was the strongest predictor of feelings of emptiness and of lower satisfaction with life and with the partner relationship.

text.text: Major financial decisions, which were usually shared, were associated with lower partner satisfaction, which suggests that decision-making power can carry demands of its own.
In Daminger's (2019) study, women undertook more anticipation and monitoring, while decision-making was more evenly shared.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Daminger's (2019)</ref> study, women undertook more anticipation and monitoring, while decision-making was more evenly shared.

text.text: Holding responsibility for care therefore does not automatically confer equivalent power over how it is organized, and the two can be configured in several ways within the same household.

The distinction between task execution and coordinating responsibility becomes especially consequential when delegation requires reminders, contingency plans, or continued responses to institutional queries.
In such arrangements, sharing visible activity can leave the obligation to ensure completion concentrated on one person.
The question is therefore which components of a care need change hands and who remains answerable if it is not met.
Answering these questions requires keeping three terms apart.

In this article, cognitive labor refers to the activities involved in organizing care, mental load to the continuing cognitive and emotional demand that this work imposes, and distress to a possible psychological consequence.
The distinction prevents the demand from being defined by its adverse outcome, since planning can be valued, performed competently, and experienced as rewarding.
The concern here is the unequal and insufficiently supported obligation to remain responsible.

This obligation falls unequally on women, and its allocation is notably resistant to changes in time and resources. Yavorsky et al. (2015) followed highly educated dual-earner couples who had shared housework relatively equally before the birth of their first child.
text.formatted: This obligation falls unequally on women, and its allocation is notably resistant to changes in time and resources. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Yavorsky et al. (2015)</ref> followed highly educated dual-earner couples who had shared housework relatively equally before the birth of their first child.

text.text: After the birth, mothers' daily workload rose by about two hours and fathers' by about 40 minutes, while both partners perceived their additional work as similar. Weeks et al. (2025), in a survey of 2,133 partnered heterosexual parents in the United States, found that women's employment and earnings were associated with less physical household labor and with no comparable reduction in cognitive labor, a pattern they describe as gendered cognitive stickiness. Offer (2014) showed that mental labor about family extends into the working day and that it was associated with negative emotions and stress among employed mothers, with no comparable association among fathers.
text.formatted: After the birth, mothers' daily workload rose by about two hours and fathers' by about 40 minutes, while both partners perceived their additional work as similar. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Weeks et al. (2025)</ref>, in a survey of 2,133 partnered heterosexual parents in the United States, found that women's employment and earnings were associated with less physical household labor and with no comparable reduction in cognitive labor, a pattern they describe as gendered cognitive stickiness. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Offer (2014)</ref> showed that mental labor about family extends into the working day and that it was associated with negative emotions and stress among employed mothers, with no comparable association among fathers.

text.text: These findings concern partnered parents, mostly in the United States, which limits generalization.
Taken together, they suggest that responsibility attaches to persons through expectations of competence and accountability that persist when the resources of the household change.
Invisibility contributes to this persistence.
Planning can be described, documented, and discussed, so it is open to inquiry; what often goes unrecognized is its standing as work for which others should share responsibility.

When attentiveness is treated as a personal trait, its unequal allocation can appear natural, and the questions of whose competence is taken for granted and whose withdrawal is judged unacceptable remain unasked.
Expectations of accountability become a continuing psychological demand through processes that research on cognition and stress has described.

The perseverative cognition hypothesis proposes that worry and rumination prolong stress-related physiological activation beyond the duration of the stressor itself, linking stressors to health outcomes through repetitive thought (Brosschot et al., 2006).
text.formatted: The perseverative cognition hypothesis proposes that worry and rumination prolong stress-related physiological activation beyond the duration of the stressor itself, linking stressors to health outcomes through repetitive thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brosschot et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Research on goal pursuit shows that unfulfilled goals produce intrusive thoughts that interfere with unrelated tasks, and that forming a specific plan for completing the goal eliminates these effects (Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011).
text.formatted: Research on goal pursuit shows that unfulfilled goals produce intrusive thoughts that interfere with unrelated tasks, and that forming a specific plan for completing the goal eliminates these effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In working life, unfinished tasks at the end of the week have been linked to impaired sleep over the weekend through rumination (Syrek et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In working life, unfinished tasks at the end of the week have been linked to impaired sleep over the weekend through rumination <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Syrek et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The present model extends this reasoning to care as a hypothesis, rather than treating laboratory findings on goals as direct evidence about caregiving.
An unresolved care need may remain cognitively active while the caregiver expects to be answerable for its completion.
A specific plan can itself reduce intrusive thought (Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011); another person is not necessarily required.
text.formatted: A specific plan can itself reduce intrusive thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011)</ref>; another person is not necessarily required.

text.text: For recurring or unpredictable needs, however, a dependable person or service may make the completion arrangement credible without requiring continued personal monitoring.

The model proposes that this arrangement can reduce persistent monitoring, anticipatory vigilance, and difficulty detaching, while allowing that these processes may continue because of worry, mistrust, preference, or previous failures of care.

Whether a successor exists depends on how care is organized beyond the household. Daly and Lewis (2000) conceptualized social care as labor carried out within normative frameworks of obligation and responsibility and with financial and emotional costs, distributed across the state, the market, the family, and the community.
text.formatted: Whether a successor exists depends on how care is organized beyond the household. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Daly and Lewis (2000)</ref> conceptualized social care as labor carried out within normative frameworks of obligation and responsibility and with financial and emotional costs, distributed across the state, the market, the family, and the community.

text.text: This perspective places schools, health services, employers, and care providers among the actors that assign responsibility, hold authority over resources, and supply or withhold successors.

Purchasing help can redistribute work within an employing household while placing demands on paid workers whose own caring arrangements may remain unsupported, so a reduction in one person's burden leaves open whether the wider arrangement is equitable.
The model therefore treats institutional resources as structural antecedents alongside the household.
The caregiving stress process model (Pearlin et al., 1990) describes how such arrangements become stress for family caregivers.
text.formatted: The caregiving stress process model <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Pearlin et al., 1990)</ref> describes how such arrangements become stress for family caregivers.

text.text: It distinguishes primary stressors, the hardships anchored directly in caregiving, from secondary stressors, which include strains in roles and activities outside caregiving and intrapsychic strains involving diminished self-concepts, with coping and social support intervening at several points.
The present model shares this process view.
Within it, the model specifies the arrangements that determine whether a caregiver can relinquish monitoring, and it locates part of the spillover into other roles in the working day.

When responsibility for care follows a caregiver into paid work, it becomes a source of workfamily conflict, which Greenhaus and Beutell (1985) distinguished into three forms: time-based conflict, in which time devoted to one role makes it difficult to meet the demands of another; strain-based conflict, in which strain produced in one role affects performance in another; and behavior-based conflict, in which behaviors required in one role are incompatible with those expected in another.
text.formatted: When responsibility for care follows a caregiver into paid work, it becomes a source of workfamily conflict, which <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Greenhaus and Beutell (1985)</ref> distinguished into three forms: time-based conflict, in which time devoted to one role makes it difficult to meet the demands of another; strain-based conflict, in which strain produced in one role affects performance in another; and behavior-based conflict, in which behaviors required in one role are incompatible with those expected in another.

text.text: Time-based policy is designed to relieve time-based conflict.
Mental load corresponds more closely to strain-based conflict, which conflict theory treats as the product of role demands in general.
The present model specifies one source of that strain, responsibility held across roles, and the conditions under which it persists after time-based conflict has eased.
Ten Brummelhuis and Bakker (2012) describe work-home conflict through depletion of personal resources and enrichment through resource accumulation.
text.formatted: Ten Brummelhuis and <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Bakker (2012)</ref> describe work-home conflict through depletion of personal resources and enrichment through resource accumulation.

text.text: Their model includes contextual demands and resources and recognizes conditional influences beyond the individual.
Continuing responsibility can therefore be represented as a demand, and reliable care provision as a contextual resource.

The present model specifies the relation between these elements: practical help transfers responsibility only to the extent that it also changes who must monitor, arrange contingencies, and account for unmet needs.
This is a proposed elaboration of resource processes, whose value depends on whether it improves explanation and measurement beyond existing constructs.

The same resource logic allows for positive transfers. Greenhaus and Powell (2006) proposed that experiences in one role can improve the quality of life in another through the transfer of resources such as skills, perspectives, and positive affect.
text.formatted: The same resource logic allows for positive transfers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Greenhaus and Powell (2006)</ref> proposed that experiences in one role can improve the quality of life in another through the transfer of resources such as skills, perspectives, and positive affect.

text.text: Care coordination can build such resources, including planning skill and a sense of competence.

This possibility is one reason the model keeps mental load distinct from distress, and it suggests that coordinating work is more likely to generate transferable resources when the person who holds responsibility also holds the power to shape the arrangement.

How far care responsibilities reach into paid work also depends on boundaries between domains. Ashforth et al. (2000) describe role boundaries on a continuum from segmentation to integration and the transitions people make across them. Clark (2000) emphasizes permeability, flexibility, and border-keepers such as supervisors and partners.

(2000)</ref> describe role boundaries on a continuum from segmentation to integration and the transitions people make across them. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Clark (2000)</ref> emphasizes permeability, flexibility, and border-keepers such as supervisors and partners.

text.text: These theories already recognize that boundaries are relational and constrained.
The present model focuses on one such constraint: when institutions continue to hold a caregiver answerable, a preference for segmentation may not translate into an opportunity to stop monitoring.
The proposed contribution is to identify the care arrangement that maintains or relaxes this constraint.

Supervisors are among the border-keepers whose behavior has been measured directly. Hammer et al. (2009) developed a measure of family-supportive supervisor behaviors comprising emotional support, instrumental support, role modeling, and creative work-family management.
text.formatted: Supervisors are among the border-keepers whose behavior has been measured directly. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hammer et al. (2009)</ref> developed a measure of family-supportive supervisor behaviors comprising emotional support, instrumental support, role modeling, and creative work-family management.

text.text: Such behaviors can widen a caregiver's authority over schedules and can provide the cover that makes disengagement possible.
Recovery research, for its part, distinguishes psychological detachment, relaxation, mastery, and control as recovery experiences measured at the level of the individual (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007).
text.formatted: Recovery research, for its part, distinguishes psychological detachment, relaxation, mastery, and control as recovery experiences measured at the level of the individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The model draws on this work and adds a structural precondition: detachment is an experience, and the opportunity to disengage is a property of the arrangement that determines whether that experience is available for a given care need.
Figure 1 summarizes the model at three levels.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref> summarizes the model at three levels.

text.text: Structural antecedents comprise social position, institutional and workplace resources, and the distribution of responsibility, authority, and the opportunity to disengage.
Psychological mechanisms comprise persistent monitoring, anticipatory vigilance, and difficulty detaching.
Consequences comprise distress, exhaustion, work-family interference, and insufficient recovery.
These levels distinguish the organization of care from its psychological experience and possible outcomes; they do not imply that every pathway has already been demonstrated.

At the first layer of antecedents, social position covers gender, socioeconomic condition, family composition, and institutional recognition, and institutional resources cover public care provision, employment conditions, workplace practices, leave and flexibility provisions, and the administrative routines of schools, health services, and other providers.

An intersectional approach examines how these positions jointly shape the relations that follow. Crenshaw (1991) shows that frameworks organized around a single axis can miss inequalities that do not fit their categories, and Collins (2019) develops intersectionality as critical inquiry into connected relations of power.
text.formatted: An intersectional approach examines how these positions jointly shape the relations that follow. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Crenshaw (1991)</ref> shows that frameworks organized around a single axis can miss inequalities that do not fit their categories, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Collins (2019)</ref> develops intersectionality as critical inquiry into connected relations of power.

text.text: In the model, each position is read as a set of arrangements that produce particular responsibilities and possibilities for action, and none serves as a general index of psychological weakness.
These positions and resources shape three relations among the people and institutions involved in a care need.
Responsibility means being answerable for anticipating needs, ensuring they are met, and accounting for outcomes when arrangements fail.
Authority is the power to define adequate care, revise decisions, and command the money, schedules, information, and cooperation needed to respond.
The opportunity to disengage is an arrangement in which a caregiver can cease personal monitoring of a specified need because responsibility is dependably assumed elsewhere.
It is bounded by the need, the period, and the agreed contingencies, rather than requiring the permanent transfer of a caring relationship.

Responsibility and authority correspond to the two terms of the demand-control model, in which Karasek (1979) proposed that mental strain arises when job demands are high and decision latitude is low.
text.formatted: Responsibility and authority correspond to the two terms of the demand-control model, in which <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Karasek (1979)</ref> proposed that mental strain arises when job demands are high and decision latitude is low.

text.text: Responsibility for outcomes functions as a demand that accumulates through unmet needs, deadlines, and the prospect of being held to account, and authority corresponds to latitude over how that demand is met.
Care coordination differs from the paid job the model describes in two respects.
Authority over care is relational: it is negotiated with partners, relatives, schools, employers, and service providers, and it is rarely written into any role.
The demand is also open ended, since needs arise at unpredictable times and across several settings at once, with no shift that formally ends.
The opportunity to disengage identifies a proposed structural support for the experience of psychological detachment described by Sonnentag and Fritz (2015).
text.formatted: The opportunity to disengage identifies a proposed structural support for the experience of psychological detachment described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Sonnentag and Fritz (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Finishing paid work does not automatically end its cognitive demands, and care has no universally defined endpoint either.
A dependable successor is expected to support release from monitoring where ongoing needs require somebody to remain answerable.
This successor must have sufficient information, authority, and capacity to act, including when circumstances change.
Assistance with a task may leave all of these responsibilities with the original caregiver.
A reduction in hours can therefore leave the arrangement unchanged, while a limited period of reliable succession may permit a meaningful interval of disengagement.
During the working day, schedule control influences whether a caregiver can respond to a need without negotiating each interruption.
Supervisors act as border-keepers, and familysupportive behaviors can supply practical assistance and workable adjustments (Clark, 2000; Hammer et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Supervisors act as border-keepers, and familysupportive behaviors can supply practical assistance and workable adjustments <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Clark, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hammer et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Cover for an employee's paid duties can reduce the simultaneous demands of work and care.
It does not by itself provide a successor for the care need.
That requires another caregiver, an employer-supported service, or another provider to assume the relevant responsibility.
Conversely, flexibility can make one worker the default contact for schools and services.
The model distinguishes these pathways so that organizational support is evaluated by what it actually changes: control of paid work, responsibility for care, or both.

The model connects these relations to persistent monitoring of known needs, anticipatory vigilance for needs that have not yet arisen, and difficulty setting that engagement aside during paid work, rest, or sleep.
Together, they describe the sustained experience of care-related mental load examined here.

The formulation builds on perseverative cognition and goal-pursuit research (Brosschot et al., 2006; Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011), but does not establish a distinct cognitive process merely by specifying its object as care.
text.formatted: The formulation builds on perseverative cognition and goal-pursuit research <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brosschot et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011)</ref>, but does not establish a distinct cognitive process merely by specifying its object as care.

text.text: Difficulty detaching corresponds to low psychological detachment (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007).
text.formatted: Difficulty detaching corresponds to low psychological detachment <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The added explanatory question concerns how the arrangement of answerability sustains these experiences, alongside individual tendencies and the objective unpredictability of needs.
Persistent monitoring and vigilance are proposed to contribute to distress, exhaustion, workfamily interference, and insufficient recovery.

Research on perseverative cognition provides a rationale for associations with sustained activation and health (Brosschot et al., 2006); workfamily conflict and recovery research identify related pathways across roles and into rest (Greenhaus & Beutell, 1985; Sonnentag & Fritz, 2015; Syrek et al., 2017).

text.text: These sources support the proposed links without establishing every pathway for care coordination.

The same coordinating activities can generate skills, meaning, and positive transfers under supportive conditions (Greenhaus & Powell, 2006; Wayne et al., 2023), so mental load should not be defined solely by adverse outcomes.
text.formatted: The same coordinating activities can generate skills, meaning, and positive transfers under supportive conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Greenhaus & Powell, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Wayne et al., 2023)</ref>, so mental load should not be defined solely by adverse outcomes.

text.text: The model combines established ideas with more specific relational definitions.
It must therefore demonstrate added value without treating different terminology as evidence of a new construct.
Empirical redundancy is a documented concern in organizational research (Le et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Empirical redundancy is a documented concern in organizational research <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Le et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Table 1 sets out the definitions, their closest conceptual neighbors, and the distinctions that would need to be tested.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> sets out the definitions, their closest conceptual neighbors, and the distinctions that would need to be tested.

text.text: Responsibility is treated as a particular demand defined by answerability, which may persist at low levels of personal task performance.
Authority is a care-specific expression of control distributed across household members and institutions.
The opportunity to disengage describes the arrangement supporting detachment, whereas detachment is the person's experience.
These distinctions do not establish independence from demands, control, support, or boundary management.

Their value depends on whether indicators of answerability and reliable succession explain variation beyond established measures, including the dimensions of invisible family load described by Wayne et al. (2023).
text.formatted: Their value depends on whether indicators of answerability and reliable succession explain variation beyond established measures, including the dimensions of invisible family load described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Wayne et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: Authority and the opportunity to disengage can act as antecedents, mediators, or moderators, depending on the arrangement of care, and the conditions under which each role applies can be stated in advance.
The opportunity to disengage can have a direct association with monitoring where responsibility is otherwise similar but reliable succession differs.
When succession varies across days, it may also condition the association between mental load and recovery.

A mediated pathway is proposed where institutions repeatedly direct information and follow-up to the caregiver recognized as responsible: concentrated contact may reduce opportunities to hand over monitoring, contributing to difficulty detaching.
These are distinct hypotheses requiring temporal ordering and appropriate comparison groups.
A single cross-sectional association cannot distinguish them, and studies should specify the intended pathway before analysis.

Authority acts as a moderator in the sense of the demand-control model: when the responsible person also holds authority over the resources that determine responses, responsibility is expected to translate less strongly into persistent monitoring and vigilance, because problems can be resolved and closed.

Evidence for this buffering interaction in the demand-control literature is weak overall, while additive effects of demands and control are consistent; buffering appears mainly when demands and control are matched on the same dimension (Häusser et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Evidence for this buffering interaction in the demand-control literature is weak overall, while additive effects of demands and control are consistent; buffering appears mainly when demands and control are matched on the same dimension <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Häusser et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The model therefore specifies authority over the resources relevant to the particular care need, which corresponds to this matching principle, and it allows for additive effects of authority as well.
Authority also acts as a mediator.

Income, secure employment, and institutional recognition confer authority over money, schedules, and dealings with services, so part of the association between social position and the psychological mechanisms is expected to run through authority.
Finally, authority can act as an antecedent of vigilance under one condition, for which the available evidence is indirect.

When authority over consequential decisions is concentrated in the same person who holds responsibility, decisionmaking may add demands of its own. Ciciolla and Luthar (2019) found that financial decisionmaking was associated with lower partner satisfaction, a finding consistent with this possibility, although it concerns relationship satisfaction and leaves vigilance unmeasured.

text.text: Authority is therefore expected to buffer strain when it matches responsibility and may add to it when it concentrates consequential decisions on a person who already carries the coordinating role.

text.text: When provisions transfer responsibility for identifying, responding to, and following up care needs, they are associated with reduced monitoring and difficulty detaching for the previous holder of responsibility.
Individual leave taken alone, reliable services, and shared institutional contact are candidate arrangements; their effects depend on whether the transfer actually occurs.

Flexibility provisions that increase a caregiver's availability without transferring responsibility can increase that caregiver's responsibility and reduce the opportunity to disengage, particularly when availability makes the caregiver the default contact for schools and services.
Proposition 4d.
Schedule control and dependable cover for paid duties reduce competing work demands and widen caregivers' authority over their working time.
A further reduction in personal monitoring of care is expected when workplace support also enables a dependable person or service to assume the relevant care responsibility.
Proposition 5a.

Gendered expectations of competence and accountability allocate responsibility for monitoring to women more than authority over resources, widening the gap between responsibility and authority (Ciciolla & Luthar, 2019; Daminger, 2019; Weeks et al., 2025).

text.text: Proposition 5b.

Higher income and secure employment expand authority and the opportunity to disengage through purchased services, schedule control, and the capacity to use paid and unpaid entitlements, while low income and precarious employment restrict them; part of the association between socioeconomic condition and the psychological mechanisms is therefore expected to run through authority (Chieregato, 2020; Chung, 2022).

text.text: Proposition 5c.
Lone caregivers and caregivers of dependents with complex or continuing needs have fewer potential successors and face more open-ended responsibility, which lowers their opportunity to disengage.

When institutions do not recognize a caregiver's relationship or family form, the caregiver holds less authority in dealings with those institutions and assumes added responsibility for securing recognition, a demand that minority stress research links to the psychological work of navigating unsupportive environments (Frost & Meyer, 2023; Meyer, 2003; Rivas-Koehl et al., 2023).

text.text: The propositions hold within boundary conditions.
Authority can bring demanding decisions, and close monitoring can reflect a chosen commitment.
Shared responsibility generates coordination costs, and added services can generate administrative work.
Continuing involvement in care can be rewarding under supportive conditions.
Evidence should therefore examine how obligations are negotiated and experienced, and should avoid inferring strain from the presence of care or ease from the language of choice.

Job demands-resources theory, the work-home resources model, and conservation of resources theory can accommodate cognitive demands, social support, control, and unequal access to resources (Bakker & Demerouti, 2017; Hobfoll, 1989; ten Brummelhuis & Bakker, 2012).

text.text: They do not require strain to fall whenever physical task time falls, because responsibility can remain a demand.
Likewise, recovery theory does not guarantee detachment merely because time away from paid work is available (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2015).
text.formatted: Likewise, recovery theory does not guarantee detachment merely because time away from paid work is available <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Sonnentag & Fritz, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The contribution proposed here is therefore one of specification: identifying when an intervention changes task execution, the distribution of answerability, or the opportunity to cease monitoring, and how those changes are connected.

Research on cognitive labor has already established its invisibility, persistence, and unequal allocation (Daminger, 2019; Dean et al., 2022). Wayne et al. (2023) further distinguish managerial, cognitive, and emotional dimensions and show that their implications need not be uniformly negative.

text.text: The present model builds on these contributions by making the transfer of responsibility a focal object of explanation.
It asks whether one caregiver can reduce monitoring because another actor assumes identification, follow-up, and contingencies, and which institutional arrangements make that handover credible.
The novelty claim concerns this proposed mechanism and its evaluation in policy, rather than the discovery that care extends beyond visible tasks.
Three linked mechanisms organize the account.
First, continued answerability may maintain monitoring after task delegation.
Second, credible succession may reduce monitoring by giving the caregiver grounds to expect that needs and contingencies will be addressed.
Third, authority over relevant resources may help convert formal responsibility into an actionable arrangement.
Succession is narrower than general support: a supportive person may provide comfort or practical help while leaving the original caregiver answerable for every outcome.
It is also distinguishable from trust alone, because confidence without sufficient capacity or authority may fail when a need changes.
Whether these distinctions add explanatory value must be tested against established measures and plausible alternatives.
Table 2 presents comparisons that separate the proposed mechanism from task time and general resource availability.
Existing theories can often accommodate both conditions in each comparison; the table therefore identifies what is specified rather than assigning them unsupported predictions.
The key question is whether measuring the transfer of responsibility improves explanation beyond task redistribution, support, control, and established dimensions of invisible family load.
The central mechanism would be weakened if reliable measures of answerability and succession were indistinguishable from existing constructs and added no explanatory value.

It would also be challenged if adequately powered longitudinal or experimental studies showed comparable reductions in monitoring after task-only redistribution and after a credible transfer of responsibility, while accounting for care needs and relevant resources.
Differences between leave taken alone and concurrently are informative only if the arrangements differ in responsibility transfer; leave configuration alone is an imperfect proxy.
A null result for a conditional pathway, such as the proposed cost of concentrated decision authority, would challenge that pathway rather than automatically refute the whole model.
Conversely, monitoring that persists after a well-supported transfer would require examination of worry, mistrust, care preferences, and previous service failures.
Tests should specify meaningful effect sizes and measurement assumptions in advance; statistical non-significance alone does not establish equivalence.
The policy implications of the model follow from Propositions 4a to 4c.
European work-life balance policy combines labor market objectives with commitments to gender equality, and its provisions set minimum entitlements to time and to requests for flexibility.

The analysis addresses sufficiency, a question distinct from what the instrument presupposes: predominantly temporal instruments may be insufficient, on their own, to transfer responsibility, and the three propositions specify the conditions under which they contribute to such a transfer.

In the terms of Greenhaus and Beutell (1985), time-based provisions address time-based conflict, and their reach into strain-based interference depends on whether a grant of time is accompanied by a transfer of monitoring, by authority over the resources that meet care needs, or by a dependable successor.

text.text: In the model's terms, leave taken alone is a route to a dependable successor for the other caregiver, and leave taken concurrently can leave the existing allocation of monitoring unchanged.
Whether an entitlement transfers responsibility depends on who can use it and how.
Chieregato (2020) identifies limits to the inclusiveness of the European framework.
Chung (2022) shows how flexible working can reproduce gendered inequalities even when it increases discretion.

Flexibility may increase boundary permeability and make a caregiver the default contact, but its effects depend on work demands, household practices, and institutional routines (Ashforth et al., 2000; Clark, 2000).

text.text: The model therefore treats flexibility as an arrangement with conditional effects, rather than assuming either benefit or harm.
Cover for paid duties and succession in care should be measured separately when evaluating workplace support.
Outside the workplace, administrative routines can keep responsibility in place.
A school or health service may record one person as the default contact and direct information, reminders, and follow-up to that person.

A grant of leave leaves that standing in place, and the burden of being the permanent point of contact eases when institutional routines distribute information and responsibility to more than one responsible person.

text.text: For each main form of leave, labor flexibility, workplace practice, and support service, it states the proposed effects on responsibility, authority, and the opportunity to disengage, the possible adverse effects, and the indicators needed to evaluate whether a transfer of responsibility has occurred.
The effects in the matrix are proposals that depend on design, payment, and implementation.
Testing begins with measurement. Wayne et al. (2023) provide an established measure of managerial, cognitive, and emotional family load against which the proposed indicators should be evaluated.
text.formatted: Testing begins with measurement. <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Wayne et al. (2023)</ref> provide an established measure of managerial, cognitive, and emotional family load against which the proposed indicators should be evaluated.

text.text: Measures need to separate task performance from answerability, identify authority over relevant resources, and record whether another actor assumes follow-up and contingencies for a specified need and period.
General social support, perceived reliability, control, boundary management, and care-related worry are essential comparators.
Psychological outcomes can draw on adapted measures of perseverative cognition and detachment.
The opportunity to disengage should be assessed through the arrangement itself, so it is not defined by the reduction in monitoring that it is intended to explain.
Dyadic or service records could supplement individual perceptions.
With measures in place, each proposition calls for a design matched to its form.
Daily diary designs with multilevel analysis suit Propositions 2a and 3b, since moderation can be examined within persons across days that differ in authority and in the availability of a successor.
Dyadic designs suit Propositions 1, 2a, and 2b, since responsibility and authority can be held by different members of a household.
Mediation designs with repeated measures suit Propositions 3c and 5b.
Multilevel designs with employees nested in work units suit Proposition 4d, since schedule control and supervisor support vary across supervisors and teams.

Longitudinal and quasi-experimental designs around leave uptake, leave taken alone or concurrently, changes in working arrangements, and changes in service procedures suit Propositions 4a to 4c, because they allow task time and the three relations to be tracked separately before and after a change.
Comparisons across gender, socioeconomic condition, family composition, and recognition status suit Propositions 5a to 5d.
Designs should attend to prior distress and changing care needs, which shape how work is organized and how its burden is reported.
The positional propositions also call for an intersectional research agenda that involves caregivers in deciding what to measure and how to interpret findings.
Recruitment should encompass varied household arrangements and relationships between paid and unpaid care, with attention to who is routinely excluded by language, time, or access requirements.

Participatory work could identify administrative or relational labor that researchers would otherwise miss, and compensating participants keeps knowledge about invisible labor from being produced through another unrecognized demand.
For policy, the model implies evaluation criteria for work-life balance measures that extend beyond hours and uptake.

A measure can be assessed by whether it transfers monitoring along with time, whether it widens the authority of the person who holds responsibility, and whether it provides a dependable successor for the needs that caregivers monitor.
The indicators in Table 3 translate these criteria into observable quantities.

text.text: Dependable public provision, accessible information, predictable employment arrangements, and workable leave entitlements are conditions that may reduce the unequal concentration of responsibility, and each requires evaluation, since added provision and coordination can themselves generate administrative work.

In service design, procedures that allow households to name more than one responsible contact, distribute information directly, and obtain coordination support address the relation that leave entitlements leave untouched.

Such procedures must accommodate lone caregivers, chosen or extended family networks, and people who cannot safely share access with another adult, so joint access is best offered as an option for households that want it.
Workplaces can combine predictable schedules, manageable workloads, and familysupportive supervision with explicit cover for paid duties (Hammer et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Workplaces can combine predictable schedules, manageable workloads, and familysupportive supervision with explicit cover for paid duties <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hammer et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Where employers support access to care services, their continuity and ability to manage contingencies should also be evaluated.
An employee's ability to hand over a work task is different from the ability to stop monitoring a family need, and neither should be inferred from a generic flexibility entitlement.
Psychologists and organizations can combine individual support with attention to these material and relational arrangements.

Boundary-setting advice may have limited effects where disengagement carries an unresolved obligation to respond, while reliable succession may still require support for trust, communication, and adjustment.
The model integrates selected literatures and is not a systematic review or an empirical test.
Much of the underlying evidence concerns partnered parents in high-income countries;
Redistributing the time spent on care tasks need not redistribute responsibility for ensuring that care happens.
The model specifies how answerability, authority, and dependable succession may connect care arrangements to persistent monitoring, vigilance, and difficulty detaching.
It builds on existing theories of demands, resources, boundaries, and cognitive labor by identifying the transfer of responsibility as a mechanism to measure and test.
For policy and practice, the implication is to evaluate who anticipates needs, who follows them through, and who can temporarily disengage, alongside hours and leave uptake.
A grant of time may support recovery more effectively when households, workplaces, and services also make a credible transfer of responsibility possible.

translate into five propositions.
Four of them are developed through subpropositions, each corresponding to a distinct path in the figure so that it can be tested separately.
Propositions 2b and 3c are conditional: they rest on indirect evidence or on an assumption stated in the text, and they are offered for empirical examination.
Proposition 1.
Responsibility for a care need is positively associated with persistent monitoring and anticipatory vigilance, independently of the time the responsible person spends performing related tasks.
Proposition 2a.

Authority over the resources relevant to a care need moderates the association between responsibility and the psychological mechanisms, such that the association is weaker when authority matches responsibility.
Proposition 2b.
When authority over consequential decisions is concentrated in the person who also holds responsibility, authority is positively associated with anticipatory vigilance.
Proposition 3a.

A lower opportunity to disengage is associated with more persistent monitoring and greater difficulty detaching, independently of the level of responsibility, and most strongly where no successor exists for a need.
Proposition 3b.

The opportunity to disengage moderates the association between the psychological mechanisms and recovery, such that the adverse association is weaker during periods when a dependable successor assumes the monitored care needs.
Proposition 3c.

Where institutions direct communication and follow-up to the person recognized as responsible, responsibility is associated with difficulty detaching partly through a reduced opportunity to disengage.
Proposition 4a.

Provisions that reduce task time or time-based work-family interference without changing who is answerable produce smaller reductions in persistent monitoring, anticipatory vigilance, and difficulty detaching than provisions that also transfer coordinating responsibility.
